GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 is essential for male gametocyte exflagellation, with Δppm2 mutants showing complete blockage of exflagellation while maintaining normal gametocyte morphology and macrogamete emergence.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - PPM2 Is Essential for Gametocyte Sex Allocation and Ookinete Differentiation; Figure 2C; Figure 4A
supporting_quotes: One mutant, Δppm1, formed morphologically normal gametocytes (data not shown) and produced macrogametes that emerged from their host cells expressing the activation marker P28, but did not produce any ookinetes. Therefore, we assessed whether microgamete formation was affected in this mutant and found that exflagellation was completely blocked.
Although exflagellation in Δppm2 was comparable to wild-type controls and Δppm5 parasites, gametocytaemia and subsequent female gamete production were severely reduced.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 is critical for female gametocyte sex allocation, with Δppm2 parasites showing an altered female:male gametocyte ratio of approximately 1:1 compared to the normal 3:1 ratio observed in wild-type controls.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - PPM2 Is Essential for Gametocyte Sex Allocation and Ookinete Differentiation; Figure 4A
supporting_quotes: This reduced female gamete count was reflected in an altered female:male gametocyte ratio of approximately 1:1 in Δppm2 parasites, compared to 3:1 observed in wild-type controls.

Sex allocation in Plasmodium is inherently female biased (∼3.6 female gametocytes to 1 male) in order to balance the greater number of male gametes per gametocyte, hence maximizing fertilization and transmission success.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 is essential for ookinete differentiation and maturation, with Δppm2 parasites showing severe defects where the majority of the population stalled at stage II of ookinete development with bulbous shaped bodies and cytoskeletal abnormalities, and oocyst development was completely ablated.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - PPM2 Is Essential for Gametocyte Sex Allocation and Ookinete Differentiation; Figure 4B, 4C, 4D, 4G; TEM analysis
supporting_quotes: Zygote (ookinete) maturation in vitro was severely affected in Δppm2 lines compared to wild-type, with the majority of the mutant population stalled by stage II of ookinete development, and oocyst development was completely ablated.
In contrast to crescent-shaped wild-type ookinetes, the vast majority of Δppm2 ookinetes were arrested at the early retort stage II, with a bulbous shaped body and cytoskeletal abnormalities.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 functions specifically in the female lineage, as demonstrated by genetic crossing experiments where Δmap2 (male-deficient) but not Δnek2 (female-deficient) gametes formed mature ookinetes when crossed with Δppm2 mutants.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Δppm2 and Δppm5 Are Defective along the Female and Male Lineages, Respectively; Figure 4E
supporting_quotes: In genetic crosses with lines deficient in either male (Δmap2) or female (Δnek2/Δnek4) gametes, Δmap2 (but not Δnek2 gametes) formed mature ookinetes when crossed with Δppm2 mutants, indicating that PPM2 is necessary for female gamete formation, as seen for PPKL.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 is expressed throughout the parasite life cycle (asexual blood stages, schizonts, gametocytes, ookinetes, and sporozoites) and shows cytoplasmic and peripheral membrane localization in blood stage parasites.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Two Unique Plasmodial PPs Are Differentially Localized; Figure 3A, 3B, 3C
supporting_quotes: qRT-PCR and C-terminal GFP tagging together demonstrated that both PPs are present throughout the life cycle, confirming previous studies.
Subcellular fractionation of blood stage parasites confirmed a cytoplasmic and peripheral membrane localization for PPM2-GFP.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 exhibits phosphatase activity as confirmed by activity assays using 3-O-methylfluorescein phosphate (MFP) as substrate, and is itself phosphorylated in schizonts and activated gametocytes as demonstrated by 32P-orthophosphate labeling.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Two Unique Plasmodial PPs Are Differentially Localized; Figure 3D, 3E
supporting_quotes: PP activity assays using 3-O-methylfluorescein phosphate (MFP) as a substrate confirmed PPM2 and PPM5 to be active PPs.

Analysis of PPM2-GFP and PPM5-GFP using 32P-orthophosphate labeling in vivo confirmed them to be phosphorylated in schizonts (as in P. falciparum) and activated gametocytes, further implicating phosphorylation as a key regulator of PP activity.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 is N-myristoylated, as confirmed by labeling with the myristic acid analog tetradec-13-ynoic acid (YnMyr) in schizonts, identifying it as a substrate of N-myristoyl transferase.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Two Unique Plasmodial PPs Are Differentially Localized; Figure 3F
supporting_quotes: PPM2 and PPM5 proteins from schizonts were also labeled by the myristic acid analog tetradec-13-ynoic acid (YnMyr), confirming previous P. falciparum myristome studies and highlighting these PPs as substrates of N-myristoyl transferase, which is currently being investigated as a potential drug target in malaria.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 contains a predicted N-terminal myristoylation site and has long Asn-rich loops within its phosphatase domain, with computational homology modeling confirming the presence of metal coordinating residues and a loop protruding close to the active site that likely affects substrate interactions.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Two Unique Plasmodial PPs Are Differentially Localized; Figure S4
supporting_quotes: The plasmodial PPMs include three proteins containing predicted sites for N-terminal myristoylation (PPM2, PPM5, and PPM6).
Computational homology modeling of PPM2 and PPM5 confirms the presence of metal coordinating residues and showed the presence of long Asn-rich loops within the PP domain.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM2 is phylogenetically similar to human PP1G and yeast PTC2 and PTC3, and the P. falciparum ortholog (PfPP2C) is refractory to deletion and has been shown to dephosphorylate translation elongation factor 1β (EF-1β).
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species; Expression and Subcellular Localization; Discussion
supporting_quotes: PPM2 is similar to human PP1G and yeast PTC2 and PTC3.
This was surprising, as the P. falciparum ortholog of PPM2 (PfPP2C) is refractory to deletion.

The importance of this protein is strengthened by the fact that PfPP2C dephosphorylates translation elongation factor 1β (EF-1β), with mutants of EF-1β showing severe growth defects and sensitivities to elongation inhibitors in yeast.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Δppm2 parasites show reduced and highly variable DNA content in ookinetes, suggesting meiotic DNA replication was initiated but aborted prior to completion.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - PPM2 Is Essential for Gametocyte Sex Allocation and Ookinete Differentiation; Figure S5C
supporting_quotes: Analysis of Δppm2 parasites revealed a reduced but highly variable DNA content, suggesting meiotic DNA replication was initiated but aborted prior to completion, as observed previously in Δmisfit parasites and to some extent in nek4 mutant parasites.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Transmission electron microscopy of Δppm2 ookinetes revealed that the few ookinetes that did mature had normal apical membrane complex and crystalline body but showed few or no micronemes, similar to SHLP1 mutants.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Ultrastructure Analysis; Figure 4G
supporting_quotes: In the few ookinetes that did mature, the apical membrane complex appeared normal, and late-stage features such as the crystalline body were present, but there were few or no micronemes, as seen in SHLP1 mutants.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Global transcriptome analysis of Δppm2 parasites revealed dysregulation of multiple gene clusters including downregulation of genes important for membrane structure (kinesins, dyneins, imc1b), cell-cycle regulation (pdeδ and nek4), ookinete motility (gap45 and gap50), and invasion (soap, ctrp, and cdpk3).
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Global Transcript Analysis; Figure 5C, 5D; Table S3, S4
supporting_quotes: Changes included downregulation of genes important for membrane structure (kinesins, dyneins, imc1b), cell-cycle regulation (pdeδ and nek4), ookinete motility (gap45 and gap50), and invasion (soap, ctrp, and cdpk3).
Furthermore, the few mature ookinetes that did form had reduced gap50 and soap expression, potentially limiting motility, invasion, and oocyst formation.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: In activated Δppm2 gametocytes, 39 protein kinases (including nek2, nek4, pk7, gak, and cdpk3) and 17 protein phosphatases (including shlp1) were differentially expressed, and members of the AP2 transcription factor family (including ap2-o) were also differentially regulated.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Global Transcript Analysis; Figure 5C, 5D; Table S4
supporting_quotes: Members the AP2 transcription factor family implicated in gametocyte and zygote formation (including ap2-o) were also differentially regulated.

In activated Δppm2 gametocytes, 39 PKs, including ones essential for zygote development (nek2, nek4, pk7, and gak) and ookinete motility (cdpk3), were differentially expressed, whereas 17 PPs, including those associated with ookinete development such as shlp1, were differentially expressed.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Protein-protein interaction network analysis revealed that approximately 30% of differentially expressed genes in Δppm2 schizonts and activated gametocytes directly interact with PPM2, including ookinete motility proteins and protein kinases CDPK3 and PK7.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Global Transcript Analysis; Figure S6C, S6D; Table S3
supporting_quotes: Approximately 30% (top 50% network, p value = 0.0002) of the differentially expressed genes in Δppm2 schizonts and activated gametocytes were also found to directly interact with PPM2.
Several ookinete motility proteins and PKs (CDPK3 and PK7) were all found to interact directly with PPM2.

AdditionalInferences: PPM2 appears to have multiple essential functions at different developmental stages, suggesting it may regulate distinct signaling pathways in gametocytes versus ookinetes, or that it has a continuous role in female lineage development that manifests as different phenotypes at different stages.

The altered sex ratio in Δppm2 parasites suggests PPM2 may be involved in environmental sensing or kin recognition mechanisms that normally regulate sex allocation, or alternatively affects female gametocyte longevity.

The N-myristoylation of PPM2 combined with its peripheral membrane localization suggests it may function as a reversible membrane-associated signaling molecule, potentially allowing it to respond to or regulate membrane-associated signaling events.

The phosphorylation of PPM2 itself suggests it is subject to regulatory control by upstream kinases, indicating PPM2 functions within a complex phosphorylation-based signaling network rather than as a simple on/off switch.

The presence of Asn-rich loops near the active site that are atypical for PPM family phosphatases may confer unique substrate specificity to PPM2, potentially explaining its non-redundant essential functions despite the presence of other PPM family members.

The pleiotropic phenotype and broad transcriptional changes in Δppm2 mutants suggest PPM2 may function relatively upstream in signaling cascades or regulate master transcriptional regulators like AP2 factors.
The similarity of the Δppm2 microneme defect to SHLP1 mutants raises the possibility that PPM2 and SHLP1 may function in related pathways controlling microneme biogenesis or trafficking.

The fact that PfPP2C (the P. falciparum ortholog) is refractory to deletion while P. berghei PPM2 can be deleted suggests potential species-specific differences in essentiality, possibly due to differences in compensatory mechanisms or life cycle requirements between human and rodent malaria parasites.
data.ShortSummary: PPM2 is an N-myristoylated, phosphorylated protein phosphatase essential for female gametocyte sex allocation and ookinete differentiation in P. berghei, with deletion mutants showing altered 1:1 sex ratios, arrested ookinete development at stage II with cytoskeletal abnormalities and microneme defects, and dysregulation of genes controlling membrane structure, motility, invasion, and cell cycle regulation.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM8 is classified as a PPM-type protein phosphatase that is part of a group containing human and yeast pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase, representing one of the most broadly conserved PPM subclasses.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species, paragraph discussing PPM classification
supporting_quotes: The most broadly conserved is PPM8, which is part of a group containing human and yeast pyruvate dehydrogenase PP
Plasmodium PPMs and PTPs generally do not fall into well-conserved subclasses. The most broadly conserved is PPM8

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM8 shows metal coordinating residues but lacks an obvious phosphate-binding arginine or lysine, distinguishing it from other PPMs analyzed.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species, paragraph on structural analysis
supporting_quotes: computational structural analysis has further supported the presence and correct position of phosphate and metal-coordinating residues in all PPPs, NIFs, and PPMs, with the exception of PPM8, which shows metal coordinating residues but lacks an obvious phosphate-binding arginine or lysine

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM8 was successfully endogenously tagged with GFP at its C-terminus in P. berghei, indicating the protein is expressed and the gene is amenable to modification.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization; Figure 2 and Figure S2B; Table S1
supporting_quotes: we used single homologous recombination to endogenously tag each of the P. berghei PPs with the green fluorescent protein (GFP) at their C terminus
resulting in successful tagging of 29 PPs as determined by western blotting and fluorescence microscopy

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM8 was successfully deleted in P. berghei asexual blood stages, indicating it is not essential for erythrocytic stage development.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis; Figure 2C; Table S1
supporting_quotes: we attempted to delete systematically each of the 30 P. berghei PPs using double homologous recombination
resulting in successful deletion of 14 PPs (47%) as determined by detailed genotype analysis

GeneSummary.bullet_point: The Δppm8 mutant showed no observable defects throughout sexual development, sporogony, and transmission to mice, suggesting functional redundancy during these stages of the life cycle.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Phenotypic Analysis; Figure 2C; Table S2
supporting_quotes: the remaining eight mutants showed no observable defects throughout sexual development, sporogony, and transmission to mice (as assessed by blood smears 4–10 days postinfection)
suggesting functional redundancy for these PPs during these stages of the life cycle

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM8 was differentially expressed in activated Δppm5 gametocytes compared to wild-type controls.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Global Transcript Analysis; Figure 5C; Table S4
supporting_quotes: only a few PKs (such as nek2 and nek3) and PPs (ppm6 and ppm8) were differentially regulated in activated Δppm5 gametocytes

AdditionalInferences: PPM8's conservation across species and similarity to pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatases suggests it may have a metabolic regulatory role, though this was not directly tested in the study.

The unusual structural feature of PPM8 (lacking phosphate-binding arginine/lysine while retaining metal-coordinating residues) may indicate a distinct substrate specificity or regulatory mechanism compared to other PPMs.

The functional redundancy of PPM8 during blood stages and transmission stages suggests other PPMs may compensate for its loss, consistent with the general observation that 78% of PPMs could be deleted.
The differential expression of PPM8 in Δppm5 mutants suggests potential functional relationships or compensatory mechanisms between different PPM family members.
PPM8's dispensability throughout the tested life cycle stages makes it a lower priority as a drug target for blood-stage or transmission-blocking interventions.
data.ShortSummary: PPM8 is a broadly conserved PPM-type phosphatase with similarity to pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatases that is dispensable for P. berghei blood stage development and transmission, though it exhibits unusual structural features including the absence of typical phosphate-binding residues.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 is essential for microgamete (male gamete) production during sexual stage development, as Δppm1 mutants formed morphologically normal gametocytes and produced macrogametes expressing the activation marker P28, but did not produce any ookinetes and exflagellation was completely blocked.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Phenotypic Analysis paragraph; Figure 2C; Table S2
supporting_quotes: One mutant, Δppm1, formed morphologically normal gametocytes (data not shown) and produced macrogametes that emerged from their host cells expressing the activation marker P28, but did not produce any ookinetes
Therefore, we assessed whether microgamete formation was affected in this mutant and found that exflagellation was completely blocked

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 is classified as a PPM-type (metal-dependent) protein phosphatase, one of 30 phosphatases identified in the P. berghei phosphatome.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome paragraph; Figure 1
supporting_quotes: We found that the P. berghei and P. falciparum phosphatomes consist of 30 and 29 PPs, respectively, encompassing 28 direct orthologs across the 5 PP families
Plasmodium PPMs and PTPs generally do not fall into well-conserved subclasses

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 was successfully deleted from the P. berghei genome (one of 14 PPs successfully deleted out of 30 attempted), indicating it is not essential for asexual blood stage development but is required for sexual stage progression.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis paragraph; Figure 2C; Table S1
supporting_quotes: A total of 178 individual gene deletion attempts were performed (at least 4 per gene; Table S1), resulting in successful deletion of 14 PPs (47%)
Overall, we did not observe a reduced growth phenotype in mice for any of the mutants, suggesting redundancy for each during asexual blood stage development

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 functions at a similar life cycle stage to the protein kinase MAP2, which is also essential for microgamete production, suggesting coordinated regulation of male gametogenesis by reversible phosphorylation.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Conclusions paragraph; Figure 6
supporting_quotes: A number of PKs are known to have an essential role at this stage, with CDPK4, MAP2, and SRPK being essential for microgamete production
A number of PPs were shown here to be essential at similar stages of the life cycle to certain kinases (e.g., MAP2 and PPM1; PK7 and PPM5; see summary, Figure 6)

AdditionalInferences: The complete block in exflagellation suggests PPM1 acts upstream or during the process of male gamete formation, potentially regulating signaling pathways required for microgamete differentiation and flagellar assembly.
Since PPM1 is dispensable for asexual blood stages but essential for male gametogenesis, it represents a potential transmission-blocking target that would not affect parasite growth in the blood.

The parallel requirement of MAP2 kinase and PPM1 phosphatase for microgamete production suggests they may act in the same or complementary signaling pathways, possibly with PPM1 counterbalancing MAP2 activity or acting downstream to regulate specific substrates.

As a PPM-type phosphatase, PPM1 likely functions as a monomer (unlike PPP-type phosphatases that require regulatory subunits), which may explain why it could be successfully deleted while many PPP-type phosphatases were refractory to deletion.
data.ShortSummary: PPM1 is a metal-dependent protein phosphatase essential for male gamete (microgamete) production in P. berghei, with deletion mutants completely blocking exflagellation while maintaining normal gametocyte morphology, functioning at a similar stage to the MAP2 kinase in regulating sexual stage development.

supporting_quotes: only two PPs were found to be localized to a single region throughout the entire life cycle: PPM4 (the nucleus) and NIF2 (the cytoplasm)

the phosphatome is highly conserved with only three proteins without direct orthology between P. falciparum and P. berghei

AdditionalInferences: NIF2's essential nature and inability to be deleted suggests it plays a critical housekeeping role in basic cellular processes, likely related to transcriptional regulation through RNA polymerase II CTD dephosphorylation.
The consistent cytoplasmic localization across all life cycle stages suggests NIF2 may have a constitutive rather than stage-specific regulatory function.

As part of the FCP family targeting RNA polymerase II, NIF2 likely participates in transcriptional regulation, which would be essential for parasite survival and explain why it cannot be functionally compensated by other phosphatases.
data.ShortSummary: NIF2 is an essential FCP-family phosphatase in P. berghei that exhibits exclusive cytoplasmic localization throughout all life cycle stages and is refractory to genetic deletion, likely due to its critical role in dephosphorylating the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Computational structural analysis supported the presence of a bona fide phosphatase catalytic domain in NIF3, with correct positioning of phosphate and metal-coordinating residues.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species
supporting_quotes: 3D structural homology modeling supported the presence of a bona fide PP catalytic domain for all included PPs

Based on available experimental template structures with substrate, phosphate, and/or metal ions bound, computational structural analysis has further supported the presence and correct position of phosphate and metal-coordinating residues in all PPPs, NIFs, and PPMs

AdditionalInferences: NIF3's essentiality for blood stage development suggests it plays a critical, non-redundant role in parasite survival, likely through regulation of RNA polymerase II-mediated transcription.
The conservation of NIF3 between P. berghei and P. falciparum (as a direct ortholog) indicates functional importance across Plasmodium species.

Given that NIF3 could not be deleted and its substrate is the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, it likely plays a fundamental role in transcriptional regulation that cannot be compensated by other phosphatases.
NIF3 may represent a potential drug target for blood stage malaria, given its essentiality and the fact that it belongs to a phosphatase family not present or functionally distinct in the human host.
data.ShortSummary: NIF3 is an essential FCP-type phosphatase in P. berghei that is refractory to genetic deletion during asexual blood stages and likely functions in transcriptional regulation through dephosphorylation of the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain.

The nucleocytoplasmic localization pattern of NIF4 is consistent with its predicted function in regulating RNA polymerase II, which operates in the nucleus but may require cytoplasmic regulatory mechanisms.
As one of only three FCPs that could not be deleted, NIF4 likely has non-redundant functions that cannot be compensated by other phosphatases in the parasite.
NIF4 represents a potential drug target for blood-stage malaria, given its essential nature and the fact that it belongs to a phosphatase family with substrate specificity distinct from host enzymes.
data.ShortSummary: NIF4 is an essential FCP-type phosphatase in P. berghei that targets the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, shows nucleocytoplasmic localization across multiple life cycle stages, and is refractory to genetic deletion in asexual blood stages, indicating its critical role in parasite survival.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PTP2 belongs to the protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) family, one of five PP families identified in the Plasmodium phosphatome.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Figure 1 and Results section - paragraph 1
supporting_quotes: PFam domains were used to define protein sets with similarity to PPP, PTP, PPM, NIF-like, and PTP-like A families

AdditionalInferences: As PTP2 is specific to P. berghei and absent in P. falciparum, it may represent a species-specific adaptation or regulatory mechanism in rodent malaria parasites.

The successful deletion of PTP2 without observable phenotypic defects across multiple life cycle stages suggests that other phosphatases in the P. berghei phosphatome can compensate for its loss, indicating functional redundancy within the PTP family or cross-family compensation.

The lack of essentiality during liver stage development (inferred from successful mosquito biteback transmission) suggests PTP2 does not play a critical role in hepatocyte invasion or liver stage replication.

PTP2 may have evolved divergently in P. berghei or been lost in P. falciparum, potentially reflecting different host-parasite interactions or transmission dynamics between rodent and human malaria parasites.
data.ShortSummary: PTP2 is a P. berghei-specific protein tyrosine phosphatase without a P. falciparum ortholog that is dispensable for asexual blood stages, sexual development, sporogony, and transmission, indicating functional redundancy within the Plasmodium phosphatome.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM9 is the only P. berghei phosphatase that could not be successfully endogenously tagged with GFP despite 18 transfection attempts, suggesting that modification of this gene is detrimental for asexual blood stage development.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization paragraph
supporting_quotes: A total of 152 individual transfection attempts were performed, resulting in successful tagging of 29 PPs as determined by western blotting and fluorescence microscopy
Despite 18 attempts, we were unable to endogenously tag PPM9, suggesting that modification of this gene is detrimental for asexual blood stage development

GeneSummary.bullet_point: The gene is referred to as PPM9 in this study and belongs to the PPM (metal-dependent protein phosphatase) family of phosphatases.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Figure 1 and Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome paragraph
supporting_quotes: Plasmodium PPMs and PTPs generally do not fall into well-conserved subclasses
Despite 18 attempts, we were unable to endogenously tag PPM9

AdditionalInferences: The inability to tag PPM9 without affecting parasite viability suggests it may play a critical role in asexual blood stage development, distinguishing it from the 14 phosphatases (47%) that were successfully deleted without observable growth defects in mice.

PPM9 appears to be essential for normal asexual blood stage function, as even C-terminal GFP tagging (which is generally well-tolerated) could not be achieved, implying the protein may be particularly sensitive to structural modifications.
The essentiality of PPM9 during blood stages makes it a potential drug target, as it cannot be deprioritized like the nearly half of PP genes shown to be nonessential for P. berghei blood stages.
data.ShortSummary: PPM9 is the only P. berghei phosphatase refractory to GFP tagging despite 18 attempts, indicating that modification of this gene is detrimental for asexual blood stage development and suggesting an essential role during this life cycle stage.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF1 is classified as a member of the FCP (NIF-like) family of protein phosphatases in Plasmodium, which commonly target the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II as their substrate.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species, paragraph 1; Gene Disruption Analysis section, paragraph 3
supporting_quotes: PFam domains were used to define protein sets with similarity to PPP, PTP, PPM, NIF-like, and PTP-like A families.
Similarly, the inability to delete three FCPs (NIF2, NIF3, and NIF4) is not surprising, as the common substrate of FCPs is the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF1 is one of the protein phosphatases without a direct ortholog between P. falciparum and P. berghei, being present only in P. berghei.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Figure 1 and Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species
supporting_quotes: As found with the kinome, the phosphatome is highly conserved with only three proteins without direct orthology between P. falciparum and P. berghei
Proteins encoded in only one species are highlighted.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Attempts to delete NIF1 using double homologous recombination were unsuccessful, indicating that NIF1 is essential for P. berghei asexual blood stage development.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis Suggests Nearly Half of the P. berghei PPs Are Redundant during Erythrocytic Stages; Figure 2C
supporting_quotes: A total of 178 individual gene deletion attempts were performed (at least 4 per gene; Table S1), resulting in successful deletion of 14 PPs (47%) as determined by detailed genotype analysis
Similarly, the inability to delete three FCPs (NIF2, NIF3, and NIF4) is not surprising, as the common substrate of FCPs is the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF1 was successfully endogenously tagged with GFP at its C-terminus for expression and localization studies.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization of the Plasmodium PPs Is Highly Diverse; Figure 2A, 2B
supporting_quotes: Therefore, we used single homologous recombination to endogenously tag each of the P. berghei PPs with the green fluorescent protein (GFP) at their C terminus and assessed protein expression and localization at five key stages of the parasite life cycle
A total of 152 individual transfection attempts were performed, resulting in successful tagging of 29 PPs as determined by western blotting and fluorescence microscopy

AdditionalInferences: NIF1's essentiality for asexual blood stage development suggests it plays a critical role in basic cellular processes, likely related to RNA polymerase II function and transcriptional regulation.

The species-specific presence of NIF1 in P. berghei but not P. falciparum suggests potential evolutionary divergence in transcriptional regulation mechanisms between rodent and human malaria parasites.

Given that NIF1 could not be deleted and is part of the FCP family targeting RNA polymerase II CTD, it may be involved in essential transcriptional processes that cannot be compensated by other phosphatases.
NIF1 represents a potential drug target for rodent malaria, though its absence in P. falciparum limits its relevance for human malaria therapeutics.
data.ShortSummary: NIF1 is an essential, species-specific FCP family protein phosphatase in P. berghei that is refractory to genetic deletion and likely functions in RNA polymerase II-mediated transcriptional regulation during asexual blood stage development.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM6 is one of three Plasmodium PPMs containing predicted sites for N-terminal myristoylation (along with PPM2 and PPM5), and is similar to a group of plant PPMs of unknown function.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species, paragraph discussing PPM classification
supporting_quotes: The plasmodial PPMs include three proteins containing predicted sites for N-terminal myristoylation (PPM2, PPM5, and PPM6).
PPM5 and PPM6 are similar to a group of plant PPMs of unknown function

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM6 was successfully endogenously tagged with GFP at its C-terminus in P. berghei and showed variable expression and localization across the parasite life cycle.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization; Figure 2A and 2B
supporting_quotes: we used single homologous recombination to endogenously tag each of the P. berghei PPs with the green fluorescent protein (GFP) at their C terminus and assessed protein expression and localization at five key stages of the parasite life cycle
Overall, expression of each PP was highly variable, with localization falling into three major classes—localized/heterogeneous, nuclear, and cytoplasmic

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM6 was successfully deleted in P. berghei asexual blood stages, suggesting it is not essential for erythrocytic stage development.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis; Figure 2C; Table S1
supporting_quotes: A total of 178 individual gene deletion attempts were performed (at least 4 per gene; Table S1), resulting in successful deletion of 14 PPs (47%)
Overall, we did not observe a reduced growth phenotype in mice for any of the mutants, suggesting redundancy for each during asexual blood stage development

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Δppm6 mutants showed no observable defects throughout sexual development, sporogony, and transmission to mice, suggesting functional redundancy during these stages of the life cycle.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Phenotypic Analysis; Figure 2C; Table S2
supporting_quotes: the remaining eight mutants showed no observable defects throughout sexual development, sporogony, and transmission to mice (as assessed by blood smears 4–10 days postinfection)
In this study, all eight mutants gave rise to blood stage infection with a 4–5 day prepatent period in mosquito biteback experiments, suggesting little effect during liver stage development

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM6 expression was differentially regulated (downregulated) in activated gametocytes of Δppm5 mutants compared to wild-type parasites.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Global Transcript Analysis; Figure 5C; Table S4
supporting_quotes: In contrast, only a few PKs (such as nek2 and nek3) and PPs (ppm6 and ppm8) were differentially regulated in activated Δppm5 gametocytes

AdditionalInferences: The predicted N-terminal myristoylation site in PPM6 suggests potential membrane association, similar to PPM2 and PPM5, though this was not experimentally validated in this study.

The successful deletion of PPM6 (along with 6 other PPMs out of 9 total, representing 78% deletion rate) supports the hypothesis that PPMs can functionally compensate for each other, consistent with their monomeric nature and conserved catalytic domains.
The differential regulation of PPM6 in Δppm5 mutants suggests potential functional relationships or compensatory mechanisms between different PPM family members during gametocyte development.

The lack of observable phenotype in Δppm6 mutants across all tested life cycle stages suggests either true functional redundancy with other phosphatases or a role in liver stage development that was not directly assessed in this study.
data.ShortSummary: PPM6 is a myristoylation-predicted phosphatase that is dispensable for P. berghei blood stage and mosquito stage development, showing functional redundancy typical of monomeric PPM family members.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 is essential for oocyst development in the mosquito stage, with deletion mutants (Δppm5) showing severely reduced oocyst size (<40%) and numbers (<5%) compared to wild-type controls, though ookinetes developed normally and were motile.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - PPM2 Is Essential for Gametocyte Sex Allocation and Ookinete Differentiation, whereas PPM5 Modulates Oocyst Development; Figure 4C
supporting_quotes: In contrast, Δppm5 ookinetes developed normally and were motile (Figures 4B and S5A). However, oocyst development was severely affected, with reduced size (<40%) and numbers (<5%) compared to wild-type controls
No sporozoites were present 14 days postinfection, and no transmission via biteback was observed (Table S2), confirming that this PP is essential during early oocyst development.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 functions specifically in the male gametocyte lineage, as demonstrated by genetic crossing experiments where crossing Δppm5 with Δnek4 lines rescued the phenotype with mature sporozoite-containing oocysts.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Δppm2 and Δppm5 Are Defective along the Female and Male Lineages, Respectively; Figure 4F
supporting_quotes: Crossing Δppm5 with Δnek4 lines rescued the phenotype, with mature sporozoite-containing oocysts 14 days postinfection (Figure 4F), indicating the requirement for a functional ppm5 gene in the male line.
The essential requirement for a functional male lineage during oocyst development is similar to properties of the misfit gene, as is its stage of essentiality.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 is predicted to be N-myristoylated at its N-terminus and was experimentally confirmed to be myristoylated in schizonts using the myristic acid analog YnMyr, with presence in soluble, peripheral membrane, and integral membrane fractions.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Two Unique Plasmodial PPs Are Differentially Localized, Show Phosphatase Activity, and Are Phosphorylated and Myristoylated; Figure 3C, 3F
supporting_quotes: PPM5 proteins from schizonts were also labeled by the myristic acid analog tetradec-13-ynoic acid (YnMyr) (Figure 3F), confirming previous P. falciparum myristome studies and highlighting these PPs as substrates of N-myristoyl transferase

Subcellular fractionation of blood stage parasites confirmed...whereas PPM5-GFP was present in all three fractions analyzed (Figure 3C), consistent with its diffuse localization in microscopic analyses

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 exhibits phosphatase activity as confirmed by enzyme assays using 3-O-methylfluorescein phosphate (MFP) as substrate, and is itself phosphorylated in both schizonts and activated gametocytes as shown by 32P-orthophosphate labeling.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Two Unique Plasmodial PPs Are Differentially Localized, Show Phosphatase Activity, and Are Phosphorylated and Myristoylated; Figure 3D, 3E
supporting_quotes: PP activity assays using 3-O-methylfluorescein phosphate (MFP) as a substrate confirmed PPM2 and PPM5 to be active PPs (Figure 3D).

Analysis of PPM2-GFP and PPM5-GFP using 32P-orthophosphate labeling in vivo confirmed them to be phosphorylated in schizonts (as in P. falciparum) and activated gametocytes (Figure 3E), further implicating phosphorylation as a key regulator of PP activity.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 shows nuclear and membrane localization in zygotes with mostly absent cytoplasmic localization, and is expressed throughout the parasite life cycle including asexual blood stages, schizonts, gametocytes, ookinetes, and sporozoites.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization of the Plasmodium PPs Is Highly Diverse; Figure 2B, Figure 3A, 3B
supporting_quotes: PPM5 was found to show both nuclear and membrane localization in zygotes but was mostly absent from the cytoplasm (Figure 2B).
qRT-PCR and C-terminal GFP tagging together demonstrated that both PPs are present throughout the life cycle, confirming previous studies (Figures 3A and 3B).

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Ultrastructural analysis by transmission electron microscopy revealed that Δppm5 ookinetes were crescent-shaped with normal apical membrane complex but showed marked variability in microneme numbers, ranging from normal to complete absence.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Ultrastructure Analysis Shows Defects in Ookinete Formation and Differentiation in Δppm2 Mutants, whereas Δppm5 Ookinetes Showed Partial Defects in Microneme Formation; Figure 4G
supporting_quotes: Δppm5 ookinetes were crescent shaped with the apical membrane complex seen in wild-type parasites (Figures 4Giii and 4Giv), but there was marked variability in the number of micronemes, ranging from normal to none
This defect could explain the formation of only a small number of abnormal oocysts that are unable to produce sporozoites.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Transcriptional analysis of Δppm5 parasites revealed downregulation of genes associated with microneme development (soap and ctrp) and oocyst development/sporogony (cap380 and csp) in activated gametocytes, with Gene Ontology enrichment for 'microneme,' 'cytoplasm,' and 'apical part of cell.'
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Global Transcript Analysis of Δppm2 and Δppm5 Reveals Dysregulation of Genes Involved in Reversible Phosphorylation, Membrane Structure, Motility, and Invasion; Figure 5C, 5E, Figure S6A
supporting_quotes: Genes associated with microneme development (soap and ctrp), oocyst development and sporogony (cap380 and csp) were downregulated in activated Δppm5 gametocytes (Figures 5C and 5E; Table S3).
GO analysis revealed enrichment of 'microneme,' 'cytoplasm,' and 'apical part of cell' in all stages of Δppm5 analyzed (Figure S6A), corresponding well with the phenotype.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 has a cluster of positive charges close to its N-terminus that may stabilize membrane anchoring, and contains long Asn-rich loops within its phosphatase domain that protrude close to the active site and likely affect substrate interactions.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Two Unique Plasmodial PPs Are Differentially Localized, Show Phosphatase Activity, and Are Phosphorylated and Myristoylated; Figure S4
supporting_quotes: PPM5 has a cluster of positive charges close to the N terminus (underlined residues in Figure S4F), and in other proteins, such as Src family kinases, these clusters are known to stabilize membrane anchoring of the protein.

For PPM2 and PPM5, the loop regions are located at different positions in the catalytic domain...this loop is likely to affect interactions with substrates, and might be involved in substrate selection.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: Protein-protein interaction network analysis showed that approximately 28% of differentially expressed genes in Δppm5 mutants across three developmental stages directly interact with PPM5, including CDPK3, CDPK5, and SHLP2.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Global Transcript Analysis of Δppm2 and Δppm5 Reveals Dysregulation of Genes Involved in Reversible Phosphorylation, Membrane Structure, Motility, and Invasion; Figure S6
supporting_quotes: In Δppm5, approximately 28% (top 50% network, p value = 0.002) of the differentially expressed genes in the three developmental stages of Δppm5 were found to directly interact with PPM5 (Figures S6B–S6D; Table S3).
For example, the data suggest that CDPK3, CDPK5, and SHLP2 interact directly with PPM5.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 belongs to the PPM (metal-dependent protein phosphatase) family and is similar to a group of plant PPMs of unknown function, with computational homology modeling confirming the presence of metal coordinating residues in its catalytic domain.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species and Two Unique Plasmodial PPs Are Differentially Localized; Figure 1, Figure S4
supporting_quotes: PPM5 and PPM6 are similar to a group of plant PPMs of unknown function
Computational homology modeling of PPM2 and PPM5 confirms the presence of metal coordinating residues and showed the presence of long Asn-rich loops within the PP domain (Figure S4).

AdditionalInferences: PPM5 likely plays a critical regulatory role in male gametocyte development that is essential for proper oocyst formation, possibly through regulation of microneme biogenesis or function.

The N-myristoylation of PPM5 may enable reversible membrane association that is important for its function during sexual stage development, allowing it to shuttle between different cellular compartments.
The defect in microneme formation in Δppm5 ookinetes suggests PPM5 may regulate protein trafficking or organelle biogenesis pathways during ookinete maturation.

PPM5's interaction with kinases like CDPK3 and CDPK5 suggests it may function in opposition to or in coordination with these kinases to fine-tune phosphorylation-dependent signaling during sexual development.

The stage-specific essentiality of PPM5 (dispensable for blood stages and ookinete formation but essential for oocyst development) suggests it regulates processes unique to the transition from ookinete to oocyst.
The presence of PPM5 in multiple subcellular fractions and its phosphorylation status suggest its activity and localization may be dynamically regulated during the parasite life cycle.
PPM5 may represent a potential drug target for transmission-blocking interventions, given its essential role in mosquito-stage development and absence of direct human orthologs.
data.ShortSummary: PPM5 is an N-myristoylated, phosphorylated metal-dependent protein phosphatase essential for male gametocyte function and oocyst development in Plasmodium, where it regulates microneme formation and expression of genes involved in sporogony, making it a potential transmission-blocking drug target.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM4 is the only phosphatase that maintains exclusive nuclear localization throughout the entire parasite life cycle, being present in the nucleus across all five key developmental stages examined (asexual blood stages, schizonts, gametocytes, ookinetes, and sporozoites).
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization paragraph; Figure 2A and 2B
supporting_quotes: only two PPs were found to be localized to a single region throughout the entire life cycle: PPM4 (the nucleus) and NIF2 (the cytoplasm)
localization falling into three major classes—localized/heterogeneous, nuclear, and cytoplasmic

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM4 was successfully endogenously tagged with GFP at its C-terminus in P. berghei, confirming protein expression that could be detected by western blotting and fluorescence microscopy.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization paragraph; Figure S2B; Table S1
supporting_quotes: we used single homologous recombination to endogenously tag each of the P. berghei PPs with the green fluorescent protein (GFP) at their C terminus and assessed protein expression and localization at five key stages of the parasite life cycle
resulting in successful tagging of 29 PPs as determined by western blotting and fluorescence microscopy

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM4 was successfully deleted in P. berghei asexual blood stages through double homologous recombination, indicating it is not essential for erythrocytic stage development.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis paragraph; Figure 2C; Figure S3; Table S1
supporting_quotes: we attempted to delete systematically each of the 30 P. berghei PPs using double homologous recombination
resulting in successful deletion of 14 PPs (47%) as determined by detailed genotype analysis

GeneSummary.bullet_point: The Δppm4 mutant showed no observable defects in ookinete conversion, sexual stage development, sporogony, or transmission to mice, suggesting functional redundancy during these stages of the life cycle.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Phenotypic Analysis paragraph; Figure 2C; Table S2
supporting_quotes: For ten mutants, ookinete conversion showed no overt differences from wild-type parasites
the remaining eight mutants showed no observable defects throughout sexual development, sporogony, and transmission to mice (as assessed by blood smears 4–10 days postinfection)

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM4 belongs to the PPM (metal-dependent protein phosphatase) family, one of five phosphatase families identified in the Plasmodium phosphatome.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome paragraph; Figure 1
supporting_quotes: PFam domains were used to define protein sets with similarity to PPP, PTP, PPM, NIF-like, and PTP-like A families
the P. berghei and P. falciparum phosphatomes consist of 30 and 29 PPs, respectively, encompassing 28 direct orthologs across the 5 PP families

AdditionalInferences: The exclusive nuclear localization of PPM4 throughout all life cycle stages suggests it may play a regulatory role in nuclear processes such as transcription, chromatin remodeling, or cell cycle regulation, though its dispensability for blood stage development indicates functional compensation by other phosphatases.
As a member of the PPM family, PPM4 likely functions as a monomeric enzyme with metal-dependent catalytic activity, consistent with the general characteristics of PPMs described in the paper.

The successful deletion of PPM4 without observable growth defects in mice supports the paper's conclusion that PPMs generally show functional redundancy, with 7 of 9 PPMs (78%) being successfully deleted.
While PPM4 was not essential in the stages tested, its role during liver-stage development cannot be excluded, as this stage was not directly assessed in the study.
The constitutive nuclear localization pattern distinguishes PPM4 from most other Plasmodium phosphatases, which show stage-specific or dynamic subcellular localization patterns.
data.ShortSummary: PPM4 is a metal-dependent protein phosphatase that uniquely maintains exclusive nuclear localization throughout all Plasmodium life cycle stages but is dispensable for asexual blood stage development, sexual development, and transmission, suggesting functional redundancy with other phosphatases.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 is essential for microgamete (male gamete) production during sexual stage development, as Δppm1 mutants formed morphologically normal gametocytes and produced macrogametes expressing the activation marker P28, but completely failed to produce ookinetes and showed completely blocked exflagellation.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis and Phenotypic Analysis sections; Figure 2C; Table S2
supporting_quotes: One mutant, Δppm1, formed morphologically normal gametocytes (data not shown) and produced macrogametes that emerged from their host cells expressing the activation marker P28, but did not produce any ookinetes
Therefore, we assessed whether microgamete formation was affected in this mutant and found that exflagellation was completely blocked

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 is classified as a PPM-type (metal-dependent) protein phosphatase, one of 30 phosphatases identified in the P. berghei phosphatome.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species; Figure 1
supporting_quotes: We found that the P. berghei and P. falciparum phosphatomes consist of 30 and 29 PPs, respectively, encompassing 28 direct orthologs across the 5 PP families
Plasmodium PPMs and PTPs generally do not fall into well-conserved subclasses

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 was successfully tagged with GFP at its C-terminus and its expression and localization were assessed across five key life cycle stages.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization; Figure 2A, 2B; Figure S2B; Table S1
supporting_quotes: Therefore, we used single homologous recombination to endogenously tag each of the P. berghei PPs with the green fluorescent protein (GFP) at their C terminus and assessed protein expression and localization at five key stages of the parasite life cycle
A total of 152 individual transfection attempts were performed, resulting in successful tagging of 29 PPs as determined by western blotting and fluorescence microscopy

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 was successfully deleted from the P. berghei genome, indicating it is not essential for asexual blood stage development, with no reduced growth phenotype observed in mice.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis; Figure 2C; Figure S3; Table S1
supporting_quotes: A total of 178 individual gene deletion attempts were performed (at least 4 per gene; Table S1), resulting in successful deletion of 14 PPs (47%) as determined by detailed genotype analysis
Overall, we did not observe a reduced growth phenotype in mice for any of the mutants, suggesting redundancy for each during asexual blood stage development

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM1 functions at a similar life cycle stage to the protein kinase MAP2, which is also essential for microgamete production, suggesting potential complementary roles in reversible phosphorylation during male gametogenesis.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Introduction to sexual stage analysis; Discussion section; Figure 6
supporting_quotes: A number of PKs are known to have an essential role at this stage, with CDPK4, MAP2, and SRPK being essential for microgamete production
A number of PPs were shown here to be essential at similar stages of the life cycle to certain kinases (e.g., MAP2 and PPM1; PK7 and PPM5; see summary, Figure 6)

AdditionalInferences: PPM1's essential role in exflagellation suggests it may regulate signaling pathways controlling male gametocyte activation and flagellum formation, potentially through dephosphorylation of key substrates involved in microtubule assembly or motor protein function.

The complete block in exflagellation but normal gametocyte morphology indicates PPM1 acts specifically during the activation phase of male gametogenesis rather than during earlier gametocyte development.

As a PPM-type phosphatase that exists as a monomer, PPM1's specificity for male gametogenesis may be conferred through its catalytic domain structure rather than through regulatory subunits, distinguishing it from PPP-type phosphatases.

The functional relationship between PPM1 and MAP2 kinase suggests the existence of a phosphorylation-dephosphorylation cycle critical for microgamete formation, where PPM1 may counterbalance MAP2 activity on shared substrates.
data.ShortSummary: PPM1 is a metal-dependent protein phosphatase essential for male gamete (microgamete) production in P. berghei, with deletion mutants showing complete blockage of exflagellation despite normal gametocyte formation, functioning at a similar stage to the MAP2 kinase and highlighting the critical role of reversible phosphorylation in sexual stage development.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF2 was successfully endogenously tagged with GFP at the C-terminus in P. berghei and showed cytoplasmic localization exclusively throughout the entire parasite life cycle, being one of only two phosphatases with single-region localization across all stages examined.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization paragraph; Figure 2A and 2B
supporting_quotes: only two PPs were found to be localized to a single region throughout the entire life cycle: PPM4 (the nucleus) and NIF2 (the cytoplasm)
Overall, expression of each PP was highly variable, with localization falling into three major classes—localized/heterogeneous, nuclear, and cytoplasmic

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF2 was refractory to gene deletion in P. berghei asexual blood stages despite multiple attempts, indicating it is essential for parasite survival during this developmental stage.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis paragraph; Figure 2C; Table S1
supporting_quotes: A total of 178 individual gene deletion attempts were performed (at least 4 per gene; Table S1), resulting in successful deletion of 14 PPs (47%)
the inability to delete three FCPs (NIF2, NIF3, and NIF4) is not surprising, as the common substrate of FCPs is the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF2 belongs to the NIF-like (FCP) phosphatase family and is classified based on catalytic domain phylogeny, with computational structural analysis supporting the presence of correctly positioned phosphate and metal-coordinating residues.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome paragraph; Figure 1
supporting_quotes: PFam domains were used to define protein sets with similarity to PPP, PTP, PPM, NIF-like, and PTP-like A families
computational structural analysis has further supported the presence and correct position of phosphate and metal-coordinating residues in all PPPs, NIFs, and PPMs

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF2 has a direct ortholog between P. falciparum and P. berghei, demonstrating conservation of this phosphatase across human and rodent malaria species.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome paragraph; Figure 1
supporting_quotes: the P. berghei and P. falciparum phosphatomes consist of 30 and 29 PPs, respectively, encompassing 28 direct orthologs across the 5 PP families
As found with the kinome, the phosphatome is highly conserved with only three proteins without direct orthology between P. falciparum and P. berghei

AdditionalInferences: The essential nature of NIF2 during asexual blood stages, combined with its targeting of RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, suggests it plays a critical role in transcriptional regulation that cannot be compensated by other phosphatases.

The consistent cytoplasmic localization throughout all life cycle stages suggests NIF2 may have a constitutive housekeeping function related to RNA polymerase II regulation rather than stage-specific developmental roles.

As an FCP family member that is refractory to deletion, NIF2 represents a potential drug target for blood-stage malaria, particularly given that this family is not well represented in the host and has a defined substrate specificity.

The conservation of NIF2 between P. falciparum and P. berghei, combined with its essential function, suggests this phosphatase performs fundamental cellular processes critical across Plasmodium species.
data.ShortSummary: NIF2 is an essential, cytoplasm-localized FCP phosphatase that is refractory to genetic deletion in P. berghei blood stages and likely functions in transcriptional regulation through dephosphorylation of RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM9 was the only phosphatase that could not be successfully endogenously tagged with GFP despite 18 transfection attempts, suggesting that modification of this gene is detrimental for asexual blood stage development.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization paragraph
supporting_quotes: A total of 152 individual transfection attempts were performed, resulting in successful tagging of 29 PPs as determined by western blotting and fluorescence microscopy
Despite 18 attempts, we were unable to endogenously tag PPM9, suggesting that modification of this gene is detrimental for asexual blood stage development

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM9 is classified as a PPM-type (metal-dependent) protein phosphatase in P. berghei.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Figure 1 - The Plasmodium Phosphatome schematic
supporting_quotes: The 5 identified Plasmodium PP families were compared to 4,969 PP-like proteins from 44 diverse eukaryotes
Plasmodium PPMs and PTPs generally do not fall into well-conserved subclasses

AdditionalInferences: The inability to tag PPM9 without affecting parasite viability suggests it may be essential for asexual blood stage development, unlike approximately half of the other P. berghei phosphatases that were successfully deleted.

PPM9 may have structural constraints or regulatory requirements that make C-terminal GFP tagging incompatible with its function, potentially due to critical C-terminal domains or protein-protein interactions.

Since PPM9 could not be tagged, its expression profile, subcellular localization, and stage-specific functions throughout the parasite life cycle remain unknown and could not be assessed in this systematic study.
data.ShortSummary: PPM9 was refractory to C-terminal GFP tagging despite 18 attempts, uniquely among the 30 P. berghei phosphatases studied, suggesting that modification of this PPM-type phosphatase is detrimental for asexual blood stage development.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 is a protein phosphatase M (PPM) family member that is essential for oocyst development in the mosquito, with deletion mutants (Δppm5) showing severely reduced oocyst size (<40%) and numbers (<5%) compared to wild-type controls, despite producing morphologically normal and motile ookinetes.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - PPM2 Is Essential for Gametocyte Sex Allocation and Ookinete Differentiation, whereas PPM5 Modulates Oocyst Development; Figure 4C
supporting_quotes: Δppm5 ookinetes developed normally and were motile (Figures 4B and S5A). However, oocyst development was severely affected, with reduced size (<40%) and numbers (<5%) compared to wild-type controls
No sporozoites were present 14 days postinfection, and no transmission via biteback was observed (Table S2), confirming that this PP is essential during early oocyst development

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 is required in the male lineage during sexual development, as demonstrated by genetic crossing experiments where crossing Δppm5 with Δnek4 lines (female-deficient) rescued the phenotype with mature sporozoite-containing oocysts, indicating the requirement for a functional ppm5 gene in the male line.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Δppm2 and Δppm5 Are Defective along the Female and Male Lineages, Respectively; Figure 4F
supporting_quotes: Crossing Δppm5 with Δnek4 lines rescued the phenotype, with mature sporozoite-containing oocysts 14 days postinfection (Figure 4F), indicating the requirement for a functional ppm5 gene in the male line

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM5 is classified as a member of the PPM (metal-dependent protein phosphatase) family and is similar to a group of plant PPMs of unknown function, with computational structural analysis supporting the presence of metal coordinating residues but lacking an obvious phosphate-binding arginine or lysine.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species; Figure 1 and Figure S1
supporting_quotes: The plasmodial PPMs include three proteins containing predicted sites for N-terminal myristoylation (PPM2, PPM5, and PPM6). PPM5 and PPM6 are similar to a group of plant PPMs of unknown function

Based on available experimental template structures with substrate, phosphate, and/or metal ions bound, computational structural analysis has further supported the presence and correct position of phosphate and metal-coordinating residues in all PPPs, NIFs, and PPMs

AdditionalInferences: PPM5 likely plays a regulatory role in male gametocyte development that is critical for subsequent oocyst maturation, given its requirement in the male lineage and the timing of the observed phenotype.

The variability in microneme formation in Δppm5 ookinetes suggests PPM5 may regulate microneme biogenesis or maturation processes, possibly through dephosphorylation of proteins involved in secretory organelle formation.

The N-myristoylation and membrane association of PPM5, combined with its cluster of positive charges, suggests it may function as a reversible membrane-associated phosphatase that can be recruited to specific cellular locations in response to developmental signals.

The downregulation of invasion-related genes (soap, ctrp) and sporozoite-specific genes (cap380, csp) in Δppm5 activated gametocytes suggests PPM5 may be involved in priming male gametocytes for post-fertilization developmental programs.

The similarity of the Δppm5 phenotype to the misfit mutant, particularly regarding male lineage requirement and stage of essentiality during oocyst development, suggests these proteins may function in related or overlapping pathways.

The phosphorylation of PPM5 itself in both schizonts and activated gametocytes suggests its activity may be regulated by upstream kinases, potentially creating feedback loops in phosphorylation-based signaling cascades.

The presence of long Asn-rich loops within the catalytic domain that protrude near the active site may confer substrate specificity unique to Plasmodium PPMs, potentially making PPM5 a suitable drug target with limited off-target effects on host phosphatases.
data.ShortSummary: PPM5 is an N-myristoylated, phosphorylated protein phosphatase essential in the male lineage for oocyst development in Plasmodium berghei, where its deletion results in ookinetes with variable microneme defects and severely impaired oocyst formation, associated with downregulation of microneme-related and sporozoite development genes.

supporting_quotes: PFam domains were used to define protein sets with similarity to PPP, PTP, PPM, NIF-like, and PTP-like A families.
Similarly, the inability to delete three FCPs (NIF2, NIF3, and NIF4) is not surprising, as the common substrate of FCPs is the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II.

GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Expression and Subcellular Localization; Figure 2B

A total of 152 individual transfection attempts were performed, resulting in successful tagging of 29 PPs as determined by western blotting and fluorescence microscopy

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF4 gene deletion was attempted but unsuccessful, indicating it is essential for asexual blood stage development in P. berghei.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - Gene Disruption Analysis; Discussion section
supporting_quotes: A total of 178 individual gene deletion attempts were performed (at least 4 per gene; Table S1), resulting in successful deletion of 14 PPs (47%)
Similarly, the inability to delete three FCPs (NIF2, NIF3, and NIF4) is not surprising, as the common substrate of FCPs is the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: NIF4 has a direct ortholog between P. berghei and P. falciparum, indicating conservation between human and rodent malaria species.
GeneSummary.evidence_location: Results section - The Plasmodium Phosphatome Is Diverse and Largely Conserved Between Species; Figure 1
supporting_quotes: We found that the P. berghei and P. falciparum phosphatomes consist of 30 and 29 PPs, respectively, encompassing 28 direct orthologs across the 5 PP families
As found with the kinome, the phosphatome is highly conserved with only three proteins without direct orthology between P. falciparum and P. berghei

AdditionalInferences: NIF4's essentiality for asexual blood stage development suggests it plays a critical role in basic cellular processes, likely related to RNA polymerase II transcriptional regulation given its substrate specificity.
The conservation of NIF4 between P. berghei and P. falciparum suggests it performs fundamental functions required across Plasmodium species.

As a member of the FCP family targeting RNA polymerase II CTD, NIF4 likely participates in transcriptional regulation, which would explain why it cannot be deleted during blood stage development when active transcription is required.
The successful GFP tagging but failed deletion attempts indicate that while the C-terminal modification is tolerated, complete loss of NIF4 function is lethal to the parasite.
data.ShortSummary: NIF4 is an essential, conserved FCP-type phosphatase in Plasmodium that targets the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain and is refractory to genetic deletion during asexual blood stages, indicating a critical role in parasite transcriptional regulation.

GeneSummary.bullet_point: PPM8 is classified as a PPP-type protein phosphatase that is part of a group containing human and yeast pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase, representing one of the most broadly conserved PPM subclasses.

supporting_quotes: The most broadly conserved is PPM8, which is part of a group containing human and yeast pyruvate dehydrogenase PP
Plasmodium PPMs and PTPs generally do not fall into well-conserved subclasses. The most broadly conserved is PPM8
